big: Dadi is admitted to hospital for three days. The bill is ₹2 lakh. Whether the family pays it from savings or the insurer pays it directly depends on a few words on one page of the policy.

lines: I have a ₹10 lakh health policy. Does that mean the insurer will pay any bill up to ₹10 lakh?
Up to ₹10 lakh in a policy year, for what the policy covers. Let us see how a claim actually flows.

rows: Paid by you at the hospital (₹ thousand)
alt: Two sets of bars showing what the patient pays upfront and what is refunded later
caps: A ₹2 lakh bill, of which ₹10,000 is not covered.
In a cashless claim at a network hospital, the family pays only the ₹10,000.
In a reimbursement claim, the family pays ₹2 lakh first and gets ₹1.9 lakh back after the bills are checked.
Same cover, very different cash needs on the day. Know your network hospitals.

rows: The most the insurer pays in one policy year
The yearly price of the cover
Insurer pays the network hospital directly
You pay first, then claim a refund
note: The premium goes up with age, with the sum insured and with the city you live in.

q: Rohan has a ₹10 lakh sum insured. A covered bill comes to ₹12 lakh in one policy year. What happens?
opts: The insurer pays all ₹12 lakh, since the bill is covered
The insurer pays nothing, since the bill is over the limit
The insurer pays ₹6 lakh, which is half of the bill
The insurer pays up to ₹10 lakh and Rohan pays the rest
why: The sum insured is the most paid in a year. A larger bill is not paid in full.
A bill over the limit is paid up to the limit. It is not rejected in full.
There is no halving rule. The insurer pays up to the sum insured on covered costs.
Cover stops at the sum insured, so Rohan pays the remaining ₹2 lakh himself.

q: Meena is treated at a hospital that is not on her insurer's network list. What is the likely route?
opts: Cashless: the insurer pays every hospital directly anyway
Reimbursement: she pays first and claims a refund later
No claim is possible outside the network at all
She must change her insurer before she can claim
why: Direct payment needs an agreement with the hospital, which a non-network hospital lacks.
Outside the network, cashless is usually unavailable, so she pays and then claims.
A claim is still possible. It simply follows the reimbursement route.
She does not need a new insurer. The same policy handles a reimbursement claim.

q: A 25-year-old and a 55-year-old buy the same ₹10 lakh cover. What is likely about their premiums?
opts: The 55-year-old pays more, since premiums rise with age
The same, since the sum insured is the same for both
The 25-year-old pays more, since young people claim more
Premiums are fixed by the insurer's choice of colour plan
why: Older people are more likely to claim, so the premium rises with age.
Premium depends on age and city as well as the sum insured, so it is not identical.
Younger buyers generally pay less, since they are less likely to claim.
There are no colour plans. Premiums come from age, sum insured, city and plan features.

q: Why does it help to check the insurer's network hospital list before you buy?
opts: It lowers the premium by the number of hospitals listed
It makes the policy start earlier than the stated date
It shows which hospitals near you allow cashless claims
It raises the sum insured when a nearby hospital is listed
why: The list does not change the price. Premium comes from age, cover and city.
Policy start dates are fixed by the policy terms, not by the list.
Cashless treatment works at network hospitals, so check that your family's hospitals are on it.
The sum insured is chosen by you at purchase and is unrelated to the list.

pts: Sum insured is the most the insurer pays in a policy year.
Cashless means the insurer pays the network hospital. Reimbursement means you pay first.
Premiums rise with age, so starting early costs less.
